title: Pure noise
objectives: Recognise white noise from its correlogram
Test for it with the Ljung-Box test, by hand and with statsmodels

screens.title: Which have no memory?
screens.prose: Four seeded series of 500 days, A to D. Each block of bars is one series' autocorrelations at lags 1 to 12, against the band of $\pm 0.088$. Two are pure noise: independent draws with nothing to remember. Two carry memory from day to day.

params.xLabel: Lags 1 to 12 of A (blue), then of B (orange)
Lags 1 to 12 of C (blue), then of D (orange)

screens.question: Select all that apply: which two are pure noise?

options.text: A
B
options.why: B's lag-1 bar is 0.27, three times the band, and the next bars decay from it. That is memory, not a stray bar.

options.text: C
D
options.why: D starts at 0.63 and decays over five lags: a strong, steady memory.

hints.text: Memory shows as a run of bars that starts tall at lag 1 and shrinks.
Compare lag 1 across the four blocks.
B and D start well above the band at lag 1 and decay. A and C have only small, scattered bars; A has two just outside.

feedback.correct: Correct. A and C are noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at lag 1 in each panel, then at the shape of what follows.

byKey.B: You took B for noise because most of its bars are small. Its lag-1 bar is 0.27, far outside the band.

explain.text: B and D have a tall lag-1 bar and a decay after it: memory. A and C show only small, scattered bars. A has two bars just outside the band, at lags 6 and 12; the next screen asks how often pure noise does that.

screens.title: How many bars stray?
screens.prose: For pure noise each bar has a 5% chance of leaving the band, and the bars are close to independent. So the number outside, out of $m$ lags, is about Binomial($m$, 0.05). Slide $m$, the number of lags you look at.
screens.question: At $m = 20$ lags, how likely is pure noise to put at least one bar outside the band?

options.text: About 64%
About 5%
options.why: That is the chance for one bar. With 20 bars, each gets its own 5% chance.

options.text: About 100%
options.why: 20 × 5% = 100% adds the chances as if they never overlap. The shaded area is $1 - 0.95^{20}$.

options.text: About 36%
options.why: That is the chance that no bar strays, $0.95^{20} = 0.36$. The question asks for at least one.

hints.text: Set $m$ to 20 and read the shaded probability.
The shading starts at 1 bar.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the shaded area at $m = 20$, or work out $1 - 0.95^{20}$.

byKey.100: You added twenty chances of 5%. The events overlap, so use the complement: $1 - 0.95^{20}$.

explain.text: $1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.64$, and the expected count is $20 \times 0.05 = 1$. A correlogram of pure noise with a bar or two outside the band is normal. This is Hypothesis Testing's twenty tests, one false alarm, in a new place.

screens.title: White noise
screens.prose: A series with mean zero, a constant variance and no autocorrelation at any lag is **white noise**, $\varepsilon_t$. Strict white noise is also independent from day to day; the difference matters in the GARCH course. Series A and C were white noise.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which of these are white noise?

options.text: Independent draws from $N(0, 1)$, one a day
The daily changes of a random walk
An AR(1) with $\phi = 0.3$
options.why: You saw small bars and called it noise. $\rho_1 = 0.3$ is real memory: yesterday moves today.

options.text: Daily volume with a weekly pattern
options.why: Its mean depends on the weekday and its ACF spikes at lag 5. Both break white noise.

options.text: A random walk
options.why: A walk's bars sit near 1 at every lag. Its changes are white noise; it is not.

hints.text: Check each one against three promises: zero mean, constant variance, no autocorrelation.
A walk is the running sum of its shocks.
The draws and the walk's changes pass all three. The AR(1) has $\rho_1 = 0.3$, the volume a weekday mean, the walk no fixed variance.

feedback.correct: Correct. The draws, and the walk's changes, which are its draws.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each series against the three promises.

explain.text: Differencing a walk hands back its shocks, so its changes are white noise (lesson 4). The AR(1) has memory, the volume a weekly mean and the walk no fixed variance. White noise is what a good model leaves behind.

screens.title: Testing all the lags at once
screens.prose: Reading bars one at a time invites false alarms. The **Ljung-Box test** pools the first $m$ of them: $$Q = n(n + 2)\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\hat\rho_k^2}{n - k}.$$ Under white noise $Q$ is roughly $\chi^2_m$. Here are five autocorrelations from $n = 100$ days: every bar is inside the band of $\pm 0.196$.
screens.question: Compute $Q$ for $m = 5$, to 2 places, and say whether it beats the 5% critical value of $\chi^2_5$.

hints.text: Square each bar and divide by $100 - k$: the first term is $0.19^2/99$.
Lag 1 contributes the most.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square each $\hat\rho_k$, divide by $100 - k$, add, then multiply by 10,200.

explain.text: $Q = 11.70$ against 11.07, so we reject white noise with p = 0.039. No single bar left the band, but five moderate bars all on one side are unlikely from noise. The test pools weak evidence that a bar-by-bar reading throws away.

screens.title: Reading the test
screens.prose: `acorr_ljungbox(x, lags=[10])` returns a table with `lb_stat`, the $Q$, and `lb_pvalue`. For `make_wn(3)`: $Q = 5.10$, p = 0.8847. For `make_ar1(0.6, 500, 5)`: $Q = 346.5$, p below $10^{-60}$. The curve is $\chi^2_{10}$; its top 5% lies beyond 18.31.
screens.question: What does `make_wn(3)`'s p-value of 0.88 tell us?

options.text: Its first 10 autocorrelations are what white noise often produces
There is an 88% chance the series is white noise
options.why: You read p as the chance the null is true. It is the chance of a $Q$ this large or larger if the series were white noise.

options.text: Reject white noise, since 0.88 is large
options.why: Small p-values reject. A large one means $Q$ sits in the bulk of the curve, far left of 18.31.

options.text: The series is proven to have no memory
options.why: Not rejecting is not proof (lesson 3's power). A weak memory could hide in 500 days.

hints.text: Where does $Q = 5.10$ sit on the curve?
The shaded tail is the rejection region at 5%.
5.10 is in the middle of the curve: 88% of white-noise samples give a larger $Q$. No reason to reject.

feedback.correct: Correct. $Q$ is unremarkable, so we do not reject.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A p-value is the chance of a $Q$ at least this large under white noise.

byKey.prob: You read p as the probability that the null hypothesis is true. Testing, lesson 3: it is a tail area computed assuming the null.

explain.text: 88% of white-noise samples give a $Q$ above 5.10, so it is no evidence of memory. The AR(1)'s 346.5 is far beyond 18.31 and rejects. Not rejecting is not proof of white noise.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import chi2

def ljung_box_q(x, m):
    n = len(x)
    r = sample_acf(x, m)
    k = np.arange(1, m + 1)
    Q = n * (n + 2) * np.sum(r[1:] ** 2 / (n - k))
    p = chi2.sf(Q, m)
    return float(Q), float(p)
widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on seeded series from `make_wn` and `make_ar1` (already defined), against statsmodels' `acorr_ljungbox` to 4 places. The first run loads NumPy and SciPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: `r[1:]` holds lags 1 to $m$; `k` is the matching array of lags.
The first row of the table is what `make_wn(3)` at $m = 10$ must give.
`Q = n * (n + 2) * np.sum(r[1:] ** 2 / (n - k))` and `p = chi2.sf(Q, m)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. Your $Q$ and p match statsmodels to 4 places.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Drop lag 0, divide each square by $n - k$, and take the upper tail with `chi2.sf`.

explain.text: The $n(n + 2)/(n - k)$ weights correct Box and Pierce's simpler $n\sum\hat\rho_k^2$ for small samples. On 30 points of an AR(1) with $\phi = 0.3$ the test gives p = 0.69: short series have little power.

screens.title: A weekly and a fortnightly cycle?
screens.prose: Series A from the start: `make_wn(24)`, pure seeded noise. Its bars at lags 6 and 12 are 0.091 and 0.096, just outside the band. A colleague writes: "Significant autocorrelation at 6 and 12 days, a weekly-and-fortnightly cycle." `acorr_ljungbox(x, lags=[20])` gives $Q = 27.54$, p = 0.121.
screens.question: What do you tell the colleague?

options.text: Two of 20 bars outside the band is what noise does; the joint test does not reject
Agree: two significant lags, six days apart, are a cycle
options.why: You read two stray bars as a pattern. Pure noise puts at least one bar outside 64% of the time, and this series is noise.

options.text: Half agree: lag 12 is real, lag 6 is chance
options.why: You kept the taller bar. Both are within 0.01 of the band, and the pooled test sees nothing.

options.text: Test more lags, say 100, until it rejects
options.why: Searching for a lag count that rejects is p-hacking. With 100 lags the test also loses power.

hints.text: How many of 20 bars should pure noise put outside, on average?
These are the two bars the colleague means.
On average one; at least one 64% of the time. Ljung-Box pools all 20 and gives p = 0.12.

feedback.correct: That's it. Noise, and the test agrees.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the binomial count, then read the Ljung-Box p-value.

byKey.cycle: You took two bars outside the band as a cycle. Twenty bars give twenty chances of 5%, so a stray bar or two is expected.

explain.text: Twenty bars at 5% each give about one stray bar, and two is common. Pooled, $Q = 27.54$ with p = 0.121: no evidence of memory. A real weekly effect would sit at lag 5 for trading days, and would survive a new sample.

screens.title: How often the test cries wolf
screens.prose: The colleague's bar-by-bar reading raises an alarm on 64% of noise samples at 20 lags. Ljung-Box promises 5%. Check the promise by simulation: draw many white-noise samples and count how often p falls below 0.05.

With 200 samples, between 5 and 15 alarms is the usual range.
`e = rng.standard_normal(n)` and `if ljung_box_q(e, m)[1] < 0.05:`.

feedback.correct: Correct. The rates are 0.06, 0.06, 0.04 and 0.04: close to 5%.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Draw `n` values per sample from `rng`, and count p-values below 0.05.

explain.text: Your rates, 0.04 to 0.06, scatter around 0.05 as 200 samples should: the binomial sd is 0.015. One pooled test keeps its promise; twenty separate glances at bars do not.

screens.title: Uncorrelated is not independent
screens.prose: 2,000 days of seeded daily returns from the GARCH course's model, `simulate_garch(2e-6, 0.08, 0.90, 2000, 7)`; the top panel shows the first 750. Ljung-Box at 10 lags: returns $Q = 12.24$, p = 0.27; squared returns $Q = 1451$, p below $10^{-300}$.
screens.question: What do the two results say together?

options.text: Today's return does not predict tomorrow's sign, but a big move predicts more big moves
The returns are strict white noise: independent from day to day
options.why: You stopped at the first test. If the days were independent, their squares would be uncorrelated too.

options.text: The two tests contradict each other, so one is wrong
options.why: They test different series. The returns can be uncorrelated while their sizes cluster.

options.text: Returns are predictable, so a direction signal can be built
options.why: The squares carry the memory, not the signs. Size is predictable; direction is not.

hints.text: A square forgets the sign and keeps the size.
Look at the calm and the busy stretches in the top panel.
Returns pass Ljung-Box: no linear memory. Squares fail it badly: large moves cluster in time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the squared series measures.

byKey.wn: You took 'passes Ljung-Box' as 'independent'. White noise only rules out correlation; the squares show the days are linked.

explain.text: The returns are white noise in the weak sense: uncorrelated. They are not independent, because a large move today makes a large move tomorrow likelier, and the squares show it. That memory in size is what GARCH models.

screens.title: A white-noise check
screens.prose: In practice we call statsmodels. `acorr_ljungbox(x, lags=[m])` returns a one-row DataFrame; `out['lb_pvalue'].iloc[0]` is its p-value as a number. Turn it into a yes-or-no check you can run on any series.
screens.question: Complete `is_white_noise(x, m, alpha)`.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_ar1(phi, n, seed, c=0.0):
    """Seeded AR(1): x_t = c + phi * x_{t-1} + e_t, e_t ~ N(0, 1), x_0 = e_0."""
    e = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(n)
    x = np.empty(n)
    x[0] = e[0]
    for t in range(1, n):
        x[t] = c + phi * x[t - 1] + e[t]
    return x

def make_wn(seed, n=500):
    """Seeded white noise: n independent N(0, 1) draws."""
    return np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal(n)

def simulate_garch(omega, alpha, beta, n, seed):
    """Seeded GARCH(1,1) returns r and variances s2."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    z = rng.standard_normal(n)
    r = np.empty(n)
    s2 = np.empty(n)
    s2[0] = omega / (1 - alpha - beta)
    for t in range(n):
        if t > 0:
            s2[t] = omega + alpha * r[t - 1] ** 2 + beta * s2[t - 1]
        r[t] = np.sqrt(s2[t]) * z[t]
    return r, s2

hints.text: Read the p-value out of the DataFrame first.
The 30-point AR(1) passes: the test cannot see its memory.
`p = float(out['lb_pvalue'].iloc[0])` and `return bool(p >= alpha)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. The check passes noise and catches the AR(1)s with enough data.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Return True when the p-value is at least `alpha`, as a plain bool.

explain.text: `True` means "no evidence of memory at these lags", not "proven white noise". The 30-point AR(1) passes because 30 days cannot reveal $\phi = 0.3$. The GARCH pair is the reminder: check the squares too.

screens.title: The Ljung-Box test
screens.prose: You pooled the bars into one statistic: $$Q(m) = n(n + 2)\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{\hat\rho_k^2}{n - k} \;\sim\; \chi^2_m \text{ under white noise}.$$ Take $m = 10$ for daily data, or about $\ln n$. Too many lags dilute a short memory among empty ones and lose power.
screens.question: $Q(10) = 21.4$ on 500 days of returns, against a 5% point of 18.31. What follows?

options.text: Reject white noise at 5%: some linear memory is present in the first 10 lags
Lag 10 is significant
options.why: $Q$ pools all ten lags. It says memory is somewhere in them, not which lag holds it.

options.text: The returns are not independent, but they are uncorrelated
options.why: That is the GARCH pattern, found by testing the squares. Here the returns themselves fail.

options.text: Do not reject, since 21.4 is close to 18.31
options.why: Close or not, 21.4 is beyond the 5% point, so the p-value is below 0.05.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $Q$ with the critical value.

explain.text: 21.4 > 18.31, so p < 0.05 and we reject. The test says memory exists among lags 1 to 10; the correlogram then shows where.

screens.title: Before you trust a t statistic
screens.prose: A signal researcher tests whether a daily signal, 500 seeded days, has a non-zero mean. Model 1 is a constant only: its residuals give $Q(10) = 46.9$, p = 0.000001. Model 2 adds yesterday's signal, an AR(1) with $\hat\phi = 0.266$: residual $Q(10) = 10.40$, p = 0.32.
screens.question: Which model's standard errors can the researcher use as printed?

options.text: Model 2: its residuals look like white noise
Model 1: it is simpler
options.why: Simpler does not help if its residuals have memory. Its standard errors assume independent errors, which they are not.

options.text: Both: the mean is estimated the same way
options.why: Correlated errors make the usual standard error too small (Regression, lesson 11). Model 1 fails the check.

options.text: Neither: Ljung-Box cannot judge residuals
options.why: Ljung-Box on residuals is the standard check. statsmodels takes `model_df` to allow for the fitted parameters.

hints.text: Which residuals pass Ljung-Box?
Compare the two p-values.
Model 1's residuals fail (p = 0.000001); model 2's pass (p = 0.32). Only model 2's errors fit the textbook standard errors.

feedback.correct: Correct. Model 2 leaves white noise behind.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A model's standard errors assume its residuals are white noise.

byKey.one: You preferred the simpler model. Its residuals carry the AR(1)'s memory, so its t statistic overstates the evidence.

explain.text: A model is done when its residuals are white noise; then its standard errors mean what they say. Otherwise fix the model or use HAC errors (Regression, lesson 11). Daily index returns often pass this check, which is the honest efficient-markets claim: no linear predictability, though their size is predictable.

ideas: White noise has mean zero, constant variance and no autocorrelation. Its bars leave the band 5% of the time each, so a stray bar or two is normal.
Ljung-Box pools the first $m$ bars into one test, $Q \sim \chi^2_m$. Use $m$ near 10 for daily data; too many lags lose power.
Passing Ljung-Box means uncorrelated, not independent: test the squares too. A model is done when its residuals are white noise.
summary.trap: Two bars of twenty outside the band are what noise does. Pool them with Ljung-Box before calling a cycle.

quiz.prose: A broken price feed repeats the same close, £50.00, for 300 days.
quiz.question: What is its lag-1 autocorrelation?

options.text: Undefined: the variance is zero
1, since every day equals the day before
options.why: You compared days directly. $\hat\rho_k$ divides by $\sum(x_t - \bar x)^2$, which is 0 here.

options.text: 0, since nothing moves
options.why: No movement means 0 over 0, not 0. The formula has nothing to divide by.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the denominator of $\hat\rho_1$.

explain.text: Every deviation from the mean is 0, so both sums are 0 and $\hat\rho_1$ is undefined. NumPy returns `nan`. A flat stretch in data is a feed problem to fix before any test.

quiz.prose: You inspect 40 lags of a correlogram of pure white noise.
quiz.question: How many bars do you expect outside the band?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each bar has a 5% chance.

byKey.zero: You expected noise to stay inside. Each bar strays 5% of the time.
byKey.one: One is the count for 20 lags. Here there are 40.

explain.text: Each of 40 bars leaves the band with chance 0.05, so we expect $40 \times 0.05 = 2$.

quiz.prose: 30 days of a seeded AR(1) with $\phi = 0.3$ give $\hat\rho_1 = 0.41$ but Ljung-Box $Q(10) = 7.42$, p = 0.69.
quiz.question: Which reading is right?

options.text: The test has too little data to see the memory; it does not show there is none
The series has no memory
options.why: You read 'not rejected' as 'proven'. The series was built with $\phi = 0.3$.

options.text: The lag-1 bar is noise, since the test did not reject
options.why: 0.41 is outside the 30-day band of $\pm 0.36$. Pooled with nine empty lags, its signal is diluted.

feedback.correct: Correct. Low power, not no memory.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what not rejecting means.

explain.text: With 30 days, $Q(10)$ averages one real lag with nine empty ones, and the test rarely rejects. Not rejecting a null is not evidence for it.

quiz.prose: A seeded AR(1) with $\phi = 0.15$ runs for 500 days. Ljung-Box gives p = 0.008 at $m = 1$, 0.086 at $m = 10$ and 0.458 at $m = 20$.
quiz.question: Why does p rise with $m$?

options.text: The memory sits at lag 1, and extra empty lags dilute it
The memory fades as more data are used
options.why: The data are the same 500 days each time. Only the number of pooled lags changes.

options.text: The test at $m = 1$ is wrong
options.why: It is the most powerful choice here, because the memory is all at lag 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What do lags 11 to 20 add to $Q$ for an AR(1) with small $\phi$?

explain.text: $\phi^k$ is tiny beyond lag 2 for $\phi = 0.15$, so extra lags add noise to $Q$ while the degrees of freedom grow. That is why $m$ near 10, or $\ln n$, is the usual choice.
